claims.text: The simulated alloy is equiatomic FeNiCrMn, corresponding to approximately 25 at.% of each element.
Within strain rates of 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1, yield strength is governed by activation of Shockley partial dislocations.
The Shockley partial dislocations operate on {111} planes.
Loading orientation, specifically <11-1> versus <110>, determines the resolved shear stress required for dislocation nucleation.
The HCP-like regions are intrinsic stacking faults rather than a thermodynamic phase transformation.
Local chemical disorder stabilizes the intrinsic stacking faults.
The initial material is a perfect FCC single crystal with no pre-existing dislocations or vacancies.
Thermal vibrations reduce the critical resolved shear stress.
The simulated strain rates provide insufficient time for full dislocation annihilation.
Shockley partials have Burgers vectors of the 1/6<112> type and create intrinsic stacking faults on {111} planes.
Yielding occurs through nucleation of Shockley partial dislocations at stress concentrators.
Vacancy clusters or surface defects are possible dislocation-nucleation sites, but the specific site is not established.
The orientation-dependent Schmid factor determines the macroscopic yield stress.
Thermal energy lowers the energy barrier for partial-dislocation separation.
The <110> loading orientation will have a higher maximum yield stress than the <11-1> orientation.
The higher predicted yield stress for <110> loading is caused by a lower Schmid factor for the active {111}<110> slip system.
The HCP-like regions will exhibit local stacking sequences consistent with intrinsic stacking faults.
Stacking-fault-derived HCP-like regions will revert to FCC upon unloading or annealing, whereas a true HCP phase will persist.
Yield strength is relatively strain-rate insensitive in the stated high-rate regime because annihilation dynamics are limited.
No twinning or FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs within the stated validity range.

contradictions.description: The initial state is specified as vacancy-free, while vacancy clusters are proposed as possible nucleation sites. This requires vacancy clusters to form during loading, but no vacancy-generation step or mechanism is stated.
